introduction.heading: What Is Docker?
introduction.description: Docker packages an app together with everything it needs to run - the runtime, system libraries, and dependencies - into a single, portable image. That image runs the same way on your laptop, a teammate's machine, and a production server, which finally puts an end to "works on my machine." For a typical Node/React project this usually means at least two moving pieces: an image for the app itself (built from a Dockerfile) and, if the app talks to a database, a second container for that database - wired together with docker-compose so `docker compose up` starts the whole stack with one command instead of a page of manual setup instructions.

concepts.title: Image vs. Container
concepts.description: An image is a read-only, versioned template built from a Dockerfile; a container is a running (or stopped) instance of that image - the same relationship as a class and an object

concepts.title: Dockerfile
concepts.description: A plain-text recipe of instructions - FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD - that Docker executes in order, top to bottom, to produce an image

concepts.title: Layers & Caching
concepts.description: Every instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new, cached layer; Docker reuses a layer unchanged on the next build unless that instruction or anything it depends on changed, which is why instruction order matters

concepts.title: Multi-Stage Builds
concepts.description: Using one stage with the full build toolchain to compile the app, then copying only the finished output into a second, minimal stage - the compilers, dev dependencies, and source maps never ship in the final image

concepts.title: Volumes & Bind Mounts
concepts.description: A named volume is storage Docker manages for you and is the right choice for a database's data directory; a bind mount maps a folder from the host straight into the container and is mainly for live-reloading source code in development

concepts.title: Docker Compose & Service Networking
concepts.description: docker-compose.yml describes several containers as one application; every service can reach every other service by its service name as a hostname, over a private network Compose creates automatically

architecture.heading: How the Pieces Fit Together
architecture.description: A Node/React app in containers is rarely just "the app." Split it into the pieces Docker actually treats separately: the client (a React app, built once and served as static files), the api (a Node/Express server that stays running), and the db (a database with its own persistent storage) - each its own container, each with its own image, talking to each other over the network docker-compose sets up. Click a service below to see what it actually is and how it's reached.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Add a .dockerignore next to the Dockerfile before anything else - without it, `docker build` copies node_modules, .git, and dist into the build context and every build gets slower
Write a multi-stage Dockerfile: an early stage runs npm ci && npm run build with the full Node toolchain, and a final, minimal stage (e.g. nginx:alpine) copies in only the built output
Build and try the image locally: docker build -t my-app . then docker run -p 5173:80 my-app, and open the mapped port in a browser
Add a docker-compose.yml with a service per piece (client, api, db) - reference other services by their service name as the hostname, never localhost or 127.0.0.1
Pass configuration with environment: or env_file: in docker-compose.yml, and keep real secrets in a git-ignored .env file - never COPY a .env into an image
Give the database a healthcheck and make the api's depends_on use condition: service_healthy, so the api doesn't try to connect before Postgres is actually ready to accept connections
Bring the whole stack up with docker compose up --build, and use docker compose logs -f <service> to tail one container's output while you debug

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A multi-stage Dockerfile, a docker-compose.yml for app + DB, and a .dockerignore
fullExample.description: This is a complete, realistic setup for containerizing a Node/React project: a multi-stage Dockerfile that builds the React client and serves it with nginx, a docker-compose.yml that wires that client to a Node/Express api and a Postgres db, and the .dockerignore that keeps the build fast and secrets out of the image. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.

steps.label: Build stage: install dependencies in a cached layer
steps.explanation: The build stage is named build (via AS build) so a later stage can copy from it by name. Copying only package.json/package-lock.json before running npm ci means this whole layer is reused on the next build unless a dependency actually changed - editing a component file won't force a full reinstall.

steps.label: Build stage: copy source and build
steps.explanation: COPY . . happens after npm ci on purpose - it's the instruction most likely to change on every build, and placing it last means it never invalidates the (slow) dependency-install layer above it.

steps.label: Runtime stage: start a second, minimal image
steps.explanation: FROM nginx:1.27-alpine AS runtime starts a brand-new, empty stage - nothing from the build stage is carried over automatically. nginx.conf here is a small custom config; the default one doesn't know that React Router needs every unknown path to fall back to index.html.

steps.label: Runtime stage: copy only the compiled output
steps.explanation: COPY --from=build pulls files from the earlier stage by name. Only /app/dist (the built, static HTML/CSS/JS) crosses into this image - node_modules, the source tree, and the entire Node toolchain used to build it are left behind, which is most of why multi-stage images end up so much smaller.

steps.label: Expose the port and run nginx as PID 1
steps.explanation: EXPOSE 80 is documentation for humans and tooling - it doesn't publish the port by itself; that's what docker run -p or compose's ports: does. CMD runs nginx in the foreground (daemon off) so it is the container's main process and receives Docker's stop signal directly, instead of Docker killing a background process it doesn't know about.

steps.label: Compose: define the client service
steps.explanation: build: tells Compose to build the Dockerfile above instead of pulling a prebuilt image. ports: "5173:80" maps host port 5173 to the container's port 80 - depends_on only controls start order here, it does not wait for the api to be ready to accept requests.

steps.label: Compose: define the api service and point it at the db
steps.explanation: DATABASE_URL uses db - the db service's name - as the hostname, not localhost; Compose's internal DNS resolves that name to the right container automatically. The named volume api_node_modules is mounted over /app/node_modules so a host bind mount elsewhere in the compose file can't shadow it with an empty or wrong-OS folder.

steps.label: Compose: define the db service with a healthcheck
steps.explanation: healthcheck runs pg_isready inside the container itself every few seconds; the api's depends_on: condition: service_healthy above waits for this to report healthy, not just for the container process to have started - closing the classic race where the api tries to connect before Postgres has actually finished initializing.

steps.label: Compose: name the persistent volumes
steps.explanation: Any volume referenced by name in a service (like db_data: above) has to be declared once at the top level too. Because db_data is a named volume rather than a path inside the container's writable layer, the database's data survives docker compose down and every image rebuild.

steps.label: .dockerignore: keep the context small and secrets out
steps.explanation: Everything sent to the Docker daemon as the "build context" gets uploaded even if a COPY never references it, so excluding node_modules and dist keeps builds fast. Excluding .env matters even more: without it, COPY . . would happily bake real secrets into an image layer, where anyone with access to the image can still read them from a shell inside a stopped container.
